title: Does Having a Pet Really Improve Our Health?
content:
As pets have grown in popularity—with more than half the global population keeping one in their homes—they’ve inspired a perception that furry (or scaly) companions improve our health. Given that social connections with other people are paramount to our well-being, it’s not such a leap to assume that social connections with other species are valuable as well, especially with cats and dogs. However, a review study published today in PLOS One finds little evidence for any overall health “pet effect.”

Featured Video

Conducted by behavioral science researchers at universities in Switzerland and the Netherlands, the study explored physical health, social support, life satisfaction, loneliness, and psychological well-being associated with pet ownership. Data from a random sample of 2,328 adult participants were extracted from Switzerland’s annual MOSAiCH survey on health. In addition, participants completed questions about pet ownership, time spent with animals, attachment levels, and attributions of emotional support.

Read more: “Why Do Some People Look Like Their Dogs?”

The researchers then compared the 1,105 participants who reported close contact with pets—ranging from cats and dogs to small terrarium animals like fish and insects—to the 1,223 participants who lacked regular contact with pets. After controlling for demographic factors like age, gender, income, and marital status, the results showed no overall differences in perceived life satisfaction or loneliness.

Some nuances did become apparent, though. Pet owners reported poorer physical health than non-pet owners, a trend the study authors attribute partly to the higher frequency of cigarette smoking by pet owners. And paradoxically, people who felt more emotionally supported by their pet, which was disproportionately women and unmarried individuals, reported slightly more feelings of loneliness. That said, pet owners who spent more time with their animals reported higher psychological well-being than those who spent less. 

Keeping in mind that the results were correlation rather than causation, the study authors concluded that pet ownership doesn’t automatically improve people’s physical or mental health. “Instead, we found that the relationship people have with their animals is much more nuanced than a simple yes-or-no question of pet ownership,” they explained in a press release. “Pet ownership is a multidimensional construct that includes characteristics of the owner, the animal, and their relationship.”

So don’t be fooled into believing that happiness is just a new cute puppy away.

title: In the Age of AI, the Analog Restaurant Feels Radical
author: Cheri Lucas Rowlands
content:
For Eater, Bettina Makalintal reports on a refreshing trend in the restaurant industry: businesses embracing lo-fi, handwritten communications and announcements in response to the ceaseless AI slop we’re served across social media these days. From a grocery store’s hand-illustrated flyers to a burger joint’s Sharpie-scribbled menu specials, restaurants are choosing advertising with a human touch and rejecting polished AI-generated graphics.

It’s hard to think of a path of more friction than choosing to run a restaurant; why add even more friction to that? In these conditions, yes, it costs more to hire a photographer to promote your new menu than to generate one with AI, but it’s also increasingly clear that many people would rather see a badly taken, lo-fi photo than an engineered AI image. For one thing, it feels like a reflection of one’s values. To me, a restaurant that employs AI art is capitulating to the culture of slop, akin to reheating premade food from Sysco. It’s impossible to square with a value system that cares about craft and integrity.

title: Blizzard's former Battle.net lead is moving his expertise over to the Epic Games Store to 'elevate player, creator, and developer experiences'
author: Elie Gould
content:
What would it take to make you use Epic's launcher? Free games? Even better revenue for devs? Or perhaps an experience that doesn't make you want to pull your hair out? Well, Epic's already tried the first two, so now it's onto the third as it hires a new VP to oversee and hopefully fix the storefront's struggles.

Martin Keely is the new Epic Games Store VP and GM (via GamesRadar), replacing Steve Allison who left the company earlier this month to join Saber Interactive. Keely's got seven years of experience under his belt with his last role being the SVP overseeing Activision Blizzard's Battle.net launcher—the only launcher other than Steam that doesn't actively piss me off. Which is why I'm actually quite interested to see what Keely does with Epic's launcher.

While working on the Battle.net launcher, Keely oversaw "growth and record results" and is now "excited to get started with the team delivering new capabilities that elevate player, creator, and developer experiences," he explains in a LinkedIn post. "I'm truly grateful for the opportunity to play a role in shaping an open and sustainable gaming ecosystem."

I wouldn't say Battle.net is particularly innovative, but it's easy to use and clearly organised. However, Battle.net does manage far fewer games on its launcher compared to the Epic Games Store, so the two aren't easily comparable in that sense—there'll undoubtedly be new challenges ahead for Keely.

Epic's founder and CEO Tim Sweeny welcomed Keely and this next stage of progress for the Epic Games Store "as we head into the era of Unreal Engine 6 and Team Open linking up to make everything work across platforms, stores, engines, and ecosystems."

Regardless of what the future will look like, this is a clear move by Epic to try to shake things up in an attempt to bring the fight to Steam and cement its place in the future of gaming. It's too early to tell whether this shift in management will actually change anything for the better but it does seem like a step in the right direction.

Elie has previously worked at TechRadar Gaming as a staff writer and studied at JOMEC in International Journalism and Documentaries – spending their free time filming short docs about Smash Bros. or any indie game that crossed their path.

title: A Strange Continent
author: Carolyn Wells
content:
Ben Markovits, an Austin-raised writer long settled in London, returns home with his teenage son and a pair of folding bikes for a ride through the Hill Country. As they pedal from Pedernales Falls toward Salt Lick BBQ, the shifting Texas landscape prompts reflections on English density versus Texan sprawl and on the deeper divide between the two cultures. By journey’s end, Markovits is left reckoning with how places—and our idea of “home”—keep changing, even as we try to return to them, a question that lingers long after the ride is over.

I had hoped, while my kids were still kids, that we’d live in Texas for a year, that they’d know something of my childhood—not just America generally, but something about the neighborhood I grew up in and the space and the year-round warm weather that makes childhood an outdoor sport, and not an indoor one as it is in England from October onward. But it didn’t happen. My daughter is now at university, and my son, 16, is caught up in the two-year cycles of English high school exams. This means the window where this move is still possible for us has closed—except for the one week over Christmas when we fly to Austin and my kids can pretend, in the company of their American cousins, to be Texans.

title: How Bots Took Over Our Lives
author: @NewYorker
content:
During the 2016 election, much of the country was introduced to the concept of internet bots for the first time. Now, just a decade later, it feels like they’re everywhere.

July 27, 2026

Photograph by Vincent Forstenlechner / Connected Archives

All the way back in 2016, when Donald Trump won his first Presidential election, many people had trouble understanding how, exactly, it could have happened. The line of inquisition extended to the political class, where recriminations from talking heads on MSNBC about Hillary Clinton’s ineffective campaigning and tone-deaf messaging abounded. Others, though, gravitated toward a more sinister conspiracy, which involved foreign interference and a network of automated agitators spreading disinformation at scale. The bots, this emerging coalition said, were to blame for Trump’s rise.

During the past decade, so-called bots, a slippery concept from the start, have gone from a conspiratorial curiosity to a familiar force in our daily lives. In the popular imagination, they are suddenly everywhere and seem designed to annoy the hell out of people. Consider the familiar indignity of buying concert tickets only to find that, immediately after a sale opens, every ticket has been purchased by an army of bots, only to be listed on a resale site with a markup of hundreds or even thousands of dollars. This is their function: bots operate on a scale and speed that gives them an unfair advantage over humans, who have to fumble around with mouse clicks and thoughts. They hoard inventory on e-commerce sites to frustrate customers and torture retailers, and scan real-estate websites so they can send automated text messages to homeowners with lowball offers. They trawl the internet to scrape e-mail addresses and then fill inboxes with phishing attempts and spam.

But the impulse to treat bots like digital mosquitoes that need to be swatted away minimizes their role in making the internet work. At their most basic, bots are bits of programming built to run a certain function automatically until something or someone stops them. They are tools, and as much as general attitudes toward them have become negative they are most often used for mundane tasks. Still, our reflexive reaction to bots on social media is irritation and suspicion—to call something a “bot” is to label it as unthinking and nonhuman. That instinct partly originated in the blame game following Clinton’s narrow loss in the 2016 election, with the rise of a general if somewhat vague consensus that a web of coördinated political agitators based in Russia had used social-networking sites like Facebook and Twitter to sow disorder and distrust in the American electorate.

The accusation wasn’t without merit. Following Trump’s victory, the Internet Research Agency, a St. Petersburg-based “troll farm,” was accused of interfering in American elections, a detail revealed in the Mueller report. According to the report, the I.R.A. had been planning this digital-agitprop campaign for several years prior to the election, even travelling to the U.S. to take photos to use in their posts. They deployed bots to pose as American grassroots political organizers, eventually making virtual contact with Trump supporters and campaign officials, and to spread bogus headlines targeted at voters in swing states. According to the report, the I.R.A.’s strategy evolved from a generalized attempt to destabilize American politics to, per the report, “a targeted operation that by early 2016 favored candidate Trump and disparaged candidate Clinton.”

This meant that the disappointed liberals who had grown convinced that Russia tilted the election toward Trump were right—or at least half right. The degree to which the Russian efforts were effective is still an open question, and some reports have cast doubt on social media’s ability to drive political outcomes. A study published in 2023 by N.Y.U.’s Center for Social Media and Politics, in Nature Communications, found that Russian bots on Twitter had limited influence, with one per cent of users being exposed to seventy per cent of the posts created by Russian troll accounts. There was also a study conducted by professors at Dartmouth, Princeton, and the University of Exeter in 2017 which found that the majority of “fake news” promoted on sites like Facebook was being consumed by hard-line conservatives who likely would have voted for Trump anyway. But it didn’t matter. The Mueller report and the spectre of Russian influence provided an easy answer for a stunning political defeat, and the modern mythology of the bots was born.

In the years since 2016, bot networks have become only more sophisticated, and the proliferation of A.I. technology promises to widen their scope. Analysis from the internet-infrastructure giant Cloudflare estimates that nearly sixty per cent of internet traffic is nonhuman. In practice, that means that many exchanges on the internet are just bots talking to other bots in an automated loop. Years ago, as virtual assistants were first taking off, a video recording of what happened when a human asked two Alexa-equipped devices at the same time to start a psychotherapy session. They end up in an infinite recursion of questions without making any progress. Now imagine that process scaled up to the size of the internet, and you have an approximation of the bot-saturated social-media platforms. Researchers at one A.I. company estimated that of a sample of more than a million accounts on X, sixty-four per cent could be bots, a finding that requires no stretch of the imagination, given the sheer inanity of interactions on the site. Under any number of viral posts, you can find accounts responding with a sequence of increasingly brainless rehashings of the original content, like a series of photocopies that slowly deteriorate in quality.

The quantity of bots on Twitter was a key sticking point for Elon Musk during his purchase of the company in 2022, and his subsequent, unsuccessful attempt to back out of the deal. He estimated that twenty per cent of the site was made up of automated accounts, a dynamic that had overvalued Twitter and should therefore allow him to walk away from his hasty acquisition. Twitter, at that point, claimed that the ratio was closer to five per cent. But bots aren’t just sitting around talking to each other; they are also a major factor in what posts become popular, facilitating virality by clustering around certain subjects and liking and reposting specific posts, creating a flywheel of engagement that spreads whatever message someone might be amplifying.

This strategy of manufacturing a froth of interest around a given subject, from Nicki Minaj’s political perspectives to Sydney Sweeney’s jean ads, has recently been especially effective, and has moved culture-war fights from the trenches of bot-infested social networks into more mainstream channels. A New York Times investigation into the social media fracas found that there were relatively few mentions of Sweeney on X until several days after the début of her infamous American Eagle commercial, and less than ten per cent of those early posts were directly critical. It wasn’t until a couple of posts that compared the ad to Nazi eugenics propaganda ended up going viral that the outrage cycle began, and conservative influencers attempted to paint what was essentially a fringe perspective on the ad campaign as a liberal consensus.

“These episodes follow a common pattern: a small incident is framed as ‘proof’ of a broader culture war, then a mix of real users, coördinated accounts, and bots push the same talking points and narratives until it looks like a widespread response,” Emilio Ferrara, a computer-science professor at U.S.C., told me. Extreme voices with high follower counts, such as Chaya Raichik, the woman behind the right-wing X account Libs of TikTok, are usually at the center of the skirmish, and then bot networks swarm to boost the message. It’s like pouring gasoline onto a few embers, which then appears to be a bonfire. Lynnette Ng, a former bot-network researcher at Carnegie Mellon University, explained why the swarm is so effective: “Bots frequently and aggressively hit cognitive-bias triggers in their messages which push the brain to short-circuit people’s ability to reason about the information in front of them.” It doesn’t help that people struggle to decipher bots from humans in the first place during political conversations. The default heat setting for political discourse online is already so high that it tends to pressurize such conversations into a single, highly combustible layer. Bots that are designed to inflame those political disagreements are trained on those conversations and then injected back into the discourse, amplifying the feedback loop of people yelling at bots who are yelling at people, and so on.

This is easy enough to understand; bots are like automated moths to digital flame. But the rationale propelling them is a little harder to decipher. Surely, some of the motive is financial, as engagement on social-media platforms has been monetized. On X, for example, an account is able to participate in X’s revenue-sharing program as long as it is “verified”—which really just means that the owner has paid a small fee for a premium account—and the page meets minimum metrics such as having five hundred verified followers and a certain number of recent “organic” impressions. (“Organic” here means that you didn’t pay for your posts to be promoted like an ad.) There’s no quality incentive here; as long as a post is attracting eyeballs and generating ad impressions, there is a potential for payout. A bot that is programmed to maximize engagement and to interact with accounts that have lots of followers can make money for its operator by appearing next to ads in the X timeline. A.I. has made that feedback loop spin only faster: bots now learn what sort of content drives the most engagement and adjust their outputs to generate likes, reposts, and comments.

Unfortunately, the posts that get the most engagement are invariably the ones that upset us the most. Rage-baiting, as this strategy is often called, is an effective behavior to program into a bot’s temperament, since people are more likely to engage with social-media posts that challenge their beliefs than those that confirm them. Maintaining a system powered by invective discourse also seems to be a practical business model for social-media platforms. A group of researchers found that removing toxic posts from a user’s feed reduced the amount of time they spent on a given platform. The total time that users spend mindlessly scrolling is the lifeblood of social-media outlets, meaning, as Ferrara explained, that they are dealing with a “conflicting system of incentives,” since bots are good for engagement metrics that can be attractive to advertisers but also mar user experience past a certain threshold. Keeping things just toxic enough so that users scroll without getting too upset at the state of the world is the sweet spot for platforms. It’s cynical, but it’s also very good business.

The platform engineers who keep people scrolling are only one cog in the attention-capturing machine. The people who create and deploy bot networks are pulling another set of levers in their attempt to make money or influence public opinion, and conflict is very good at attracting eyeballs. Many bots on social media are trained to maximize engagement, and the number of likes, shares, or comments a post receives is a large component of how the algorithms on X, Instagram, and TikTok decide what to put in front of users next. Those two parties—the platform owners who tweak the algorithm’s currents and the bot operators who ride it—work in tandem to shape people’s experiences online and end up warping reality in the process. There’s a growing weariness about the bot-dominated internet, though. Perhaps it explains why so many people were upset when it was revealed that Geese, a band beloved by the exact kinds of people who consider their music taste to be unassailably authentic, had reportedly worked with a marketing company to create legions of fake fan accounts. This tactic is not a major deviation from decades of creative and manipulative music marketing, but coverage of the controversy was overwhelmingly negative. Critics accused the band’s label of waging a “PsyOp,” one in which bots were capable of building an alternate reality and tricking them into liking something, almost against their will.

Ng compared the mechanics behind the glut of bots inflaming culture-war topics to an automated propaganda war that is currently being won by the individuals and groups more willing to use available technologies to pursue their own ends. “They’re an interesting tool for automated advertising that can be used by people to do good and do harm. Instead of us focussing on bots that are doing harm, we should focus on how we can use the same technology to make them do good.” It’s a pragmatic solution, if a little depressing, to give over the rest of the internet to automated skirmishes against disinformation.

Personally, I’d rather let the bots fight one another and log off forever. And yet the bot revolution is coming—or is perhaps already here—whether we like it or not. It goes far beyond political discourse, as bots now dominate how we experience life online: the customer-support chatbots that pop up when you want to rebook a flight, A.I.-powered summaries at the top of Google searches, automatic censors that flag and remove explicit content. But what happens when bots are all that’s left of digital life? Such a reality doesn’t seem terribly far away. Some in Silicon Valley would hand their entire lives over to “agents,” a dressed-up term for bots which has become one of the industry’s favorite words. Agents, though, are conceived of as independent and capable of reasoning, a spin along the lines of “bots with thoughts.”

In February, a security researcher at Meta named Summer Yue created an A.I. agent using the platform OpenClaw that she tasked with managing her Gmail account and suggesting which messages she should delete. Before she knew it, the bot started deleting all the e-mails in her inbox, like a digital locust. “I couldn’t stop it from my phone. I had to RUN to my Mac mini like I was defusing a bomb,” she wrote on X. That a security researcher for Meta was comfortable handing over the keys to her e-mail account to an autonomous bot that quickly went feral was funny, but after reading Yue’s story I found myself staring at my inbox. It was Sunday afternoon, and I had just got back from a weekend away. The number of unread e-mails in my inbox hovered around eighty thousand, and I found myself fantasizing about turning my whole life over to the bots and letting an agent nuke my overflowing inbox. It sounded liberating. Perhaps that’s what the A.I. apocalypse is really shaping up to be—not the elimination of humanity by an omniscient machine mind but an internet overrun by unthinking, error-prone automatons that make the web unusable and destroy it from the inside. After the bots take over, we can all get back to the real world. ♦

title: The Return of the Monarch
author: Krista Stevens
content:
Monarch butterfly populations are on the upswing. But, faced with climate change, pine bark beetles, and even avocado-farming cartels, can it last? For The Atlantic, Vann R. Newkirk II follows Cinderella, Eric, and Carle, three butterflies named by his young daughter, as they leave their wintering ground in Mexico to migrate north to lay eggs in order to complete their “biological mission.”

Cinderella, Eric, and Carle had all been tagged in Sierra Chincua, which meant that I could deduce certain facts about their lives. They were already bona fide world-class wanderers, having flown there all the way from Canada in the fall, a three-month trip. Along the way, they’d dodged birds and windmills and cars, eventually reaching the same patch of forest—perhaps even the same trees—that their great-grandparents had roosted in. For much of the winter, they had not eaten and had barely moved, jamming themselves so tightly against their fellow travelers that from a distance they looked like scales armoring the sides of the trees. Now they’d awakened, stretching their wings and warming up.

title: The Irony and the Ecstasy of Colson Whitehead
author: @NewYorker
content:
Download a transcript.

Listen and subscribe: Apple | Spotify | Wherever You Listen

Sign up to receive our weekly cultural-recommendations newsletter.

Colson Whitehead’s ascent in the literary world has seemed, like much of what he does, impressively effortless. Though he’s best known for “The Underground Railroad” and “The Nickel Boys”—both of which were awarded Pulitzer Prizes—his œuvre also includes a mystery set amid rival schools of elevator inspectors, a zombie novel, and an autobiographical coming-of-age story. On this episode of Critics at Large, Vinson Cunningham, Naomi Fry, and Alexandra Schwartz survey Whitehead’s wide-ranging body of work. The hosts are joined by their fellow staff writer Julian Lucas, who recently profiled Whitehead for The New Yorker. Together, they discuss three central works: “The Underground Railroad,” which catapulted its author from literary darling to mainstream celebrity; “Sag Harbor,” which fictionalizes, barely, Whitehead’s summers in the Hamptons and the family dramas that played out there; and “Harlem Shuffle,” the first installment of the crime trilogy that concluded this month, with the publication of “Cool Machine.” On the page, Whitehead is a true Gen X ironist, transmitting heavy histories and themes with levity. Despite the occasional darkness of his subject matter, he’s also one of our funniest novelists. “He has this way of, almost like a standup comedian, drawing you into this playful patter,” Lucas says. “Then your defenses go down, and that’s when he hits you with something that grabs you emotionally, or that pulls you into a story.”

title: Love It or Hate It, Ferrari’s First EV Is a Thrilling Drive
author: @wired
content:
Jul 29, 2026 8:00 AM

WIRED test-drove a preproduction version of the Luce, the storied Italian automaker’s controversial electric car, and it was remarkably surprising. Will it convert Ferrari fanatics?

Courtesy of Ferrari

Some still believe that you can’t manage a car company unless you’re a fully paid-up “car guy.” Tell that to Benedetto Vigna, Ferrari’s CEO. He’s a physicist by education, hired to run the company in 2021 after a career in semiconductors, although he did significant business with automotive during that time.

Vigna also helped develop a three-dimensional motion sensor first used in airbags, later adapted for the Nintendo Wii and the iPhone’s screen rotation function. An inventor, then. “I prefer innovator,” he once told me. “A lot of the time inventors are just thinking, but innovators conceive new things and make them happen.”

This is all useful background to the Luce, Ferrari’s first fully electric car, engineered in Maranello, Italy, but designed in California by LoveFrom, the agency set up by renowned iPhone designer Jony Ive. It’s not Apple’s abandoned car, reskinned and rebooted for the world’s most famous automotive name, but more the product of a union between like-minded innovators—Italian spirit and attitude, Silicon Valley lateral thinking.

But unless you’ve been hiding under a rock on Mars with Elon Musk these past few months, you’ll also know that the result didn’t land the way its creators would have anticipated. Ferrari’s immense global fan base is seemingly not on board with the idea of an electric car on a point of principle. And hiring Ive and his team to reimagine the aesthetic has proven as welcome as Kryptonite is to Superman.

Part of the frequently obnoxious discourse around the Luce centered around the idea that a Ferrari’s design should deliver an instant dopamine rush. These aren’t cars that require a PhD in design to understand; they’re meant to hit hard and fast, seeding desire the moment you see them. The Luce spectacularly breaks from tradition, and without the famous Prancing Horse badge, there’s little here that yokes it to perhaps the most revered automotive back catalog of all. But that was all part of the brief: Do something different.

The driving experience amplifies this feeling. The Luce is a Ferrari, just not the sort we’re used to. “In the past 100 years, technology has changed for sure,” Raffaele de Simone, Ferrari’s chief test driver, tells me. “But what hasn’t changed is our bodies. We have two hands, two eyes and ears, and two feet. The interface is the same—steering, brakes and throttle—but the Luce has a different sort of driving emotion and a different way of announcing driving thrills.”

Driving Different

I was at a test track in northern Italy in May to find out how successfully that’s been achieved. I was in a preproduction car, still disguised at the time of driving because it pre-dates the car’s reveal in Rome. First impressions? The Luce’s cab-forward proportions mean you sit closer to the front axle than usual, and higher because there’s a large battery pack beneath the cabin. It’s clearly not low-slung or sporty.

You can’t help but take in that interior, clearly Apple-inspired but positing a whole new approach to territory that has seen an entire generation of new cars lose sight of first principles. The three-spoke wheel’s design is inspired by a classic Ferrari’s, and it feels fantastic. The air vents pivot with a deeply engineered precision. Even the seat runners are elegant. The space in the rear is almost limo-like.

One of Ive’s superpowers is being able to detect the level of care invested in a product's design, and whether you like the Luce’s aesthetic or not, that’s indisputable. But he rejects the concept of a touchscreen inside a car, choosing instead to elevate haptic feel and the clarity of the dials to a level previously unseen in the automotive context. Ive is all about input and output. The Luce is a special place to be.

There’s a slickness to the first driving impressions, too. Ferraris have become less highly strung over the years, with greater emphasis now placed on daily usability. As befits its four-door, five-seat layout, the Luce is arguably the most accessible Ferrari in the company’s near-80-year history. Its major controls—the throttle and brake pedal—are beautifully calibrated, so it moves away effortlessly with an impressively and perhaps unexpectedly light touch. On some classic Ferraris, you have to let the gearbox oil warm thoroughly before going anywhere. This is not an issue on the Luce, despite its complex electronic drive units.

The structure is all new. The chassis consists of hollow castings, extrusions and aluminum sheets, to reduce weight and optimize load paths. The 800-volt battery architecture is integrated into the chassis, positioned as low in the Luce’s floorpan as the engineers could achieve. So it has a center of gravity that’s 95 mm lower than the Purosangue, Ferrari’s quasi-SUV, and a yaw moment of inertia 15 percent less than that car. That means it’s more agile and changes direction more keenly.

That’s physics in play. Ferrari’s commitment to technology is greater than ever, and the Luce deploys everything it knows to manage those external forces. It enjoys unprecedented control of each wheel in all three axes (lateral, longitudinal, and vertical), with particular emphasis on lateral body dynamics. A new “vehicle control unit” oversees power delivery and energy recovery, and updates target metrics 200 times per second. As with all high-end electric vehicles, the Luce’s master controller has a lot to do.

Prancing Power

The electric Ferrari has a 122-kWh battery and four e-motors, two on each axle, and optimum weight distribution. The front motors deliver 282 brake horsepower (bhp), the rears 831 bhp, so the total output is north of 1,000 bhp. And there’s mammoth torque: 5,900 pound-feet (around 8,000 Newton-meters) at the rear wheels, a crazy amount of force.

The front motors can spin at up to 30,000 revolutions per minute and can go from nothing to maximum in less than a second. The chassis and body consist of 75 percent recycled aluminum. There’s also a separate rear subframe for the first time on a Ferrari; it’s connected to the rest of the chassis by elastomeric bushes—polymers with a high viscosity—which helps reduce noise and vibration.

A new “e-manettino” dial on the lower left of the steering wheel joins the existing one on the right, a staple of all Ferraris since its arrival in 2004’s F430 model. The new addition has three settings that govern power and traction, as well as the shape of the torque curve. In Range mode, power is limited to 429 bhp, and the car is predominantly rear-drive. Select Tour, and the driver has 608 bhp to enjoy, with all-wheel drive capability. In the Performance setting, that rises to 958 bhp, and the top speed is raised to a maximum of 190 mph.

Engineering this sort of bandwidth into an EV is nothing new. However, the application here is more emotionally charged: Ferrari has an obligation to organize the possibilities as entertainingly as possible. How else will it be able to silence that fan base seemingly intent on shunning the concept of an electric Ferrari?

“What excites me is that we have more tools available than ever before to give the driver exactly what they’re asking from the car,” de Simone tells me. “Let’s say you’re entering a corner and suddenly the radius tightens. Instantly the driver is asking the car for a little more rotation. In that moment, rear-wheel steering, active suspension, and torque vectoring from the four motors are all working together to help achieve that response. What’s interesting is that you don’t necessarily feel the individual systems at work. What you feel is confidence.”

Because it can vector torque on both axles, the Luce’s dynamic behavior plays out in hi-def widescreen. The front end is positive without being overly sensitive; it remains neutral throughout the middle phase of the corner and has incredible traction on the exit. Ferrari long ago mastered the chassis hardware, but it's a software leader now, too; its Side Slip Control system reaches v10 in the Luce, and its traction control has evolved to suit the car’s quad-motor configuration. Select Performance mode and switch the other manettino to “CT off” (traction control off), and the Luce gets distinctly more playful. It’s doubtful that many owners will ever drift their $600,000 electric Ferrari, but it can certainly do it.

Like all engineers, Ferrari’s people love graphs and charts and will happily share what they deem is proof that the 4,982-pound Luce feels significantly less than that. Subjectively, it has the alertness and willingness to change direction of a much lighter car, but given that it’s five meters long and two meters wide, you still need space to explore these limits.

Electric Shifts, Kraftwerk Sounds

Further interactivity (and graphs) arrive in the form of the Luce’s Torque Shift Engagement. This is Ferrari’s answer to one of the issues with EVs: the rather one-dimensional way that they deliver their energy. Pull the right paddle on the steering column and you get five power and torque levels; the left one delivers five grades of regenerative engine braking, with incremental illumination within the instrument display so you can keep track of the deployment.

The Luce plays with the torque curve so that you feel like you’re fully in command during cornering entry and exit rather than simply riding a huge wave of torque. In essence, it’s designed to conjure the sensation you feel driving a car with a conventional transmission and engine braking. The amount of energy corresponds with the available grip and the nature of the corner itself. It’s a step up from the synthesized gearbox in the Hyundai Ioniq 5 N and the e-shift option available in the latest Porsche Taycan, as good as they are.

The Luce’s dynamic bandwidth extends to its ride quality, even on 23- and 24-inch wheels, and on the gnarliest surfaces. It’s fitted with the third generation of Ferrari’s 48-volt active suspension and controls its mass very adroitly without ever becoming floaty.

Finally, there’s the way it sounds. Largely silent, barring some mild wind and tire noise, the Luce finds its voice in Performance mode. There’s something of the harmonic rasp of a six-cylinder to it, and it’s not quite as rumbly as a V-8, never mind a V-12. But it’s real and musical—more Kraftwerk-adjacent than Pavarotti, perhaps—and has been achieved by using an accelerometer and by equalizing naturally occurring frequencies on the rear inverter.

“You can think about it like a musical instrument. It has its own timbre,” says Antonio Palermo, who led this part of the Luce’s development team. “We need to take away the annoying noise, because there’s no point amplifying gear whine, for example. But there are lots of other beautiful frequencies we can work with and let out. We talk about orchestras when it comes to ICE. Well, there’s a different type of orchestra inside this machine, too.”

The Luce clearly repositions and reimagines the very idea of what a Ferrari could be. For most people, that’s a romantic notion likely steeped in dreams of Italy at its most seductive, or a wailing combustion engine closing in on an 8,500-rpm redline. Hence the fallout. The Luce is on a different path, and it demands an alternative response. But in terms of how it drives, there’s no question it’s authentically Ferrari. We can’t wait to drive it again.

Jason Barlow is an automotive expert and author. He is editor at large for Top Gear magazine and a contributing editor to Britain's GQ, and he writes regularly for The Sunday Times newspaper. ... Read More

title: X Says Australia’s Under-16 Social Media Ban Risks Interfering With Foreign Law
author: @wired
content:
X has a new argument against sweeping underage social media bans that would limit usage of its platform: They interfere with international law.

The social media platform, which sits within Elon Musk’s SpaceX, issued a submission to the Australian parliament published Tuesday that called for the government to drop efforts to strengthen its underage social media ban. It complained that the proposals to increase pressure on sites to demonstrate efforts to crack down on underage access are unnecessary, ill-suited, unfair, and could violate privacy rights.

X pushed back against the “highly invasive” information gathering powers the proposed amendment would allow, accusing the commissioner of having “seemingly no understanding” of how this would work for the platforms and no safeguards for confidential and commercially sensitive information. Demanding data, documents, and compliance evidence from non-Australians in other countries could cause issues “for the comity of nations,” the firm also warned.

Australia is leading a growing global movement to restrict children’s access to social media, after banning under-16-year-olds from the sites in December. In May, the country ordered X to pay a $463,000 fine for failing to comply with child safety measures. The country’s internet regulator, eSafety, first issued the fine in 2023, claiming X did not respond sufficiently to a request for information on how it was tackling the spread of online child sexual abuse content, submitted one month before Elon Musk took over Twitter, now X.

X has previously criticized the country’s “excessive” penalty regime and complained in the most recent submission that a proposal to increase penalties against individuals is “entirely unjustified and disproportionate.”

Musk has been a particularly vocal critic of Australia’s bill to make 16 the minimum age for social media. “Seems like a backdoor way to control access to the Internet by all Australians,” he wrote on X when the legislation was announced in late 2024. When Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez announced similar measures in February of this year, Musk called him a “tyrant” and “true fascist totalitarian.”

While many digital rights campaigners believe blanket age bans on social media are “problematic,” the information-gathering powers are not the issue, says Stefania Di Stefano, a researcher in international law and technologies.

“For me, the complete ban from social media on children and minors is problematic from an international human rights perspective,” says Di Stefano. “It is disproportionate with respect to the right of children to exercise their right to freedom of expression, their right to access information, their right to association, and so on and so forth.”

But Julia Hörnle, a professor of internet law at Queen Mary University of London, is skeptical about X’s submission. “A regulator in Australia ordering X to disclose a document in relation to their business activities in Australia, that’s perfectly fine,” she tells WIRED. “From all the data in the possession of the social media company, they can distinguish between Australian and non-Australian children, and therefore keep regulation to Australia.”

title: UN expert warns that border policies cannot override the absolute ban on deportation to torture
content:
News

UN expert warns that border policies cannot override the absolute ban on deportation to torture

A UN expert warned on Tuesday that policies on border protection and migration cannot nullify the absolute ban on returning a person to torture as set out in international law.

The UN Special Rapporteur on torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, Alice Jill Edwards, published a position paper on the principle of non-refoulement to torture. The paper stipulates that this principle is one of the “most important safeguards in international human rights law,” emphasizing that it creates an absolute prohibition of torture, without exception.

The non-refoulement principle prohibits States from “transferring or removing individuals from their jurisdiction or effective control when there are substantial grounds for believing that the person would be at risk of irreparable harm,” including torture.

Edwards responded to the recent moves made by governments, such as the United States and United Kingdom, to “accelerate removals” and  “expand third-country return arrangements.” She warned that policies or bilateral deals must not contravene the non-refoulement principle, as externalizing asylum processing to third countries does not absolve a nation of its legal duty to protect vulnerable individuals from being returned to a dangerous and potentially life-threatening situation.

On 1 June 2026, the Council of the EU approved the Return Regulation whose powers include the expansion countries of return and return hubs,  and the expansion of entry bans. The UK government also recently announced plans to incorporate AI facial recognition technology to assess younger asylum seekers’ ages.

Edwards elaborated that while states do have the “right to control their borders” and remove those who have not followed legal processes, they cannot return persons to torture. She reiterated the importance of fair assessments of every person facing removal, warning that diplomatic assurances “must never become paper promises used to legitimise an otherwise unlawful return.”

Her warning comes amidst a time of global turbulence for refugees and asylum seekers, with Egyptian authorities forcibly deporting Sudanese nationals fleeing armed conflict, which results in them having to live in an active war zone where they face a compounded risk of being subjected to extrajudicial killings, and torture. In India, strict border enforcement policies that saw a naval vessel cast Rohingya refugees adrift into the Andaman Sea in May 2025 was decried by rights groups as a direct contravention of this principle.

Although many states have justified their acts of forcibly returning asylum seekers to dangerous situations as an act to control their border security and have emphasized that since they are not signatories to the 1951 UN Refugee Convention, they are not under any legal obligation to do so, Edwards notes that it is important for them to comply by their obligations under customary international law.
